newsitem.title: USA: Political foes argue against casinos in Mass..
newsitem.headline: Political foes argue against casinos in Mass..

text.p: Massachusetts's leading law enforcement official joined forces with his political foe, the state treasurer, to warn lawmakers that casino gambling will cost Massachusetts money and damage residents' quality of life.

Attorney General Scott Harshbarger, the first witness before a Government Regulations Committee hearing Tuesday at the State House, called various plans to increase gambling in Massachusetts "short sighted economic policy", "bankrupt social policy," and "a mirage."
"I'm not saying casinos represent the decline of civilization, but they certainly are not our finest hour," said Harshbarger, a Democrat and probable contender in the 1998 gubernatorial election.

Treasurer Joseph Malone, a Republican and also a possible 1998 candidate, cited a 1996 study concluding that if casinos are legalized, Massachusetts residents will spend $1 billion more a year on wagering than they do now.
The state's Lottery revenues will suffer, he said.

Committee members considered all 18 bills now pending on Beacon Hill relating to gaming in Massachusetts. The most visible is the 1995 agreement or "compact" between Gov. William F. Weld and Cape Cod's Wampanoag tribe to open a full casino in New Bedford.

Weld's compact is a package of three bills, allowing for the construction of the Wampanoag casino, a casino in Hampden County, and the installation of 700 slot machines at each of the state's four race tracks.
